newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Sick Russian general arrested on graft charges.
newsitem.headline: Sick Russian general arrested on graft charges.

text.p: One of Russia's highest ranking generals, a hero of the 1991 coup, was forced out of hospital on Wednesday and hauled off to Moscow's notorious Lefortovo prison for interrogation on corruption charges, military prosecutors said.

In a drama charged with echoes of Stalin's purges of 60 years ago, General Konstantin Kobets, who defended President Boris Yeltsin during the hardline communist putsch of August 1991, complained the Kremlin was making a scapegoat of a sick man and said he feared for his life in prison.

"With this...struggle against corruption they need a trial that will create a lot of noise and they need to stitch someone up in a big way," Kobets told Ekho Moskvy radio from the clinic where he was being treated after a mild heart attack.
"I feel very bad, both physically and mentally," he said.

In sharp contrast to the 1930s, however, Yeltsin's anti-corruption campaign is based on well-founded suspicions. It has the support of ordinary Russians who believe top officials have plundered state resources on a grand scale.

Such is the extent of a recent wave of military sackings for corruption that a Kremlin Defence Council meeting on Thursday to discuss army reform may have to concentrate on filling vacancies left by disgraced generals and admirals.
A spokesman for the military prosecutors' office told Reuters that Kobets, a deputy defence minister charged with abusing his authority, had been arrested and taken to Lefortovo.

The grim jail housed generations of political prisoners under the tsars and in Soviet times. Thousands of Stalin's victims, many of them high-ranking military personnel, were shot there during the purges, which reached their peak in 1937.

"I'm absolutely and precisely aware that if they lock me up in custody, I won't survive more than 10 or 20 days there," Kobets, 57, told Ekho Moskvy before he was taken away. "They'll try to get rid of me -- a knife in the back, and that's it."
Kobets has denied accusations that he accepted gifts, including a luxurious country dacha, from a building contractor paid by the army and which employed the general's son.
In a courtesy rarely extended to the unfortunate prisoners of the 1930s, Kobets was reported to have been allowed to return to his dacha to pick up a change of clothing.

Kobets said he believed Yeltsin, who briefly made him defence minister after he marshalled a few hundred troops to defend the beleaguered democrats in Moscow's White House in 1991, had been misled by his advisers into sacking him.
"I don't know where the pressure is coming from although I can guess that this action has been provoked, planned and very precisely directed," he said.
Other senior officers facing graft charges have accused rivals in the hierarchy of conspiring to have them removed.

Military prosecutors say as many as 20 generals and 100 colonels are under investigation for graft. Stories abound of army stores, from rations to rockets, being sold off for private profit and of defence contractors building lavish country dachas for the top brass in exchange for lucrative army orders.
The situation is all the more sensitive as the vast majority of the forces 1.8 million officers and men live on the breadline. Morale is low and suicides are commonplace.
